message.content:
**Earliest Non‑Christian Historical Mention**

The first known reference to Jesus Christ outside Christian writings comes from the Jewish historian **Flavius Josephus** in his work *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 18, Chapter 3), written around **AD 93–94**. In this passage—often called the “Testimonium Flavianum”—Josephus briefly describes Jesus as a wise man who performed miracles, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and had followers who continued after his death.

> *“Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man; for he was a doer of wonderful works… He was crucified by Pilate, but his disciples did not abandon their faith.”*  
> — *Antiquities of the Jews*, 18.3.2 (cited in many modern translations)

This passage is widely accepted by scholars as containing an authentic core, though later Christian editors may have added or embellished certain phrases. It predates other secular references such as those by the Roman historian **Tacitus** (*Annals* 15.44, c. 116 CE) and the Roman writer **Pliny the Younger** (*Letters* 10.96, c. 112 CE).

So, the earliest surviving historical record that mentions Jesus Christ is Josephus’ *Antiquities*, dated to the late 90s CE.
